food_cultures.summary_en: Koganei is a center of the movement to preserve and popularize historic Tokyo vegetable varieties. Its farmers, markets, and municipally recognized restaurants connect Edo-period agricultural heritage with present-day food.

facts.claim_en: The name Edo-Tokyo Vegetables originated with a Koganei community revitalization group, and at least nine recognized varieties are cultivated in the city.
Koganei certifies restaurants that incorporate Edo-Tokyo vegetables into their dishes.
facts.source_title: 小金井市認定 江戸東京野菜使用店

food_cultures.summary_en: This juicy, sweet heritage melon traces its wider ancestry to makuwa cultivation under the Tokugawa government. Koganei farmers revived it, giving the variety its modern local identity.

facts.claim_en: Koganei farmers restored this heritage makuwa melon, which is eaten as a sweet fruit.
JA recognizes Koganei Makuwa as an Edo-Tokyo heritage crop linked to local seed preservation.

makers.name_ja: 小金井市内の復活栽培農家
makers.relation_en: Local growers revived and maintained the melon.

food_cultures.notes_en: The variety is specifically tied to Koganei, unlike many heritage vegetables whose original place names refer to other Tokyo districts.

food_cultures.name_ja: シントリ菜（ちりめん白菜）
food_cultures.summary_en: A crisp Edo-Tokyo leafy vegetable historically prized for its tender inner stalks. Its use in refined soups links the crop to older Tokyo cooking.

facts.claim_en: Shintori-na is grown in Koganei; its crisp stalk centers were traditionally selected for soup dishes in high-end restaurants.

food_cultures.summary_en: Norabo is a historic leafy brassica valued for its edible stalks, leaves, and buds. Accounts of its role during past famines give the vegetable particular regional significance.

facts.claim_en: Norabo is among the heritage greens cultivated in Koganei; historically its seeds provided oil while its tender greens served as food.

food_cultures.summary_en: This large, thick-rooted heritage daikon has a texture suited to simmered Japanese dishes. Its cultivation in Koganei extends a vegetable tradition originally developed elsewhere in Tokyo.

facts.claim_en: Traditional Okura daikon is cultivated in Koganei and is particularly suitable for oden and other simmered dishes.

food_cultures.summary_en: A relatively short, pointed white daikon associated historically with eastern Tokyo. Koganei cultivation helps preserve a variety traditionally used in light pickles and other preparations.

facts.claim_en: Kameido daikon is grown as a heritage variety in Koganei; its comparatively dry flesh suits pickling and frying.

food_cultures.summary_en: This heritage cucumber has a pale lower half and greener upper half. Its distinctive appearance and relatively firm flesh make it part of Tokyo's traditional pickling culture.

facts.claim_en: Koganei cultivates Magome half-white cucumber, a Meiji-period variety traditionally suited to rice-bran pickles.

food_cultures.summary_en: A small, dense heritage eggplant associated with the former Terajima district. It is one of the Tokyo heirlooms maintained by growers in Koganei.

facts.claim_en: Koganei grows Terajima eggplants, whose compact flesh suits grilling and simmering after frying.

food_cultures.summary_en: A small Tokyo heritage turnip cultivated in Koganei as part of its Edo-Tokyo vegetable preservation effort.

facts.claim_en: Kanamachi small turnip is explicitly listed among the Edo-Tokyo heritage vegetables grown in Koganei.

food_cultures.summary_en: A short-rooted carrot developed in the Tokyo area during the modern era. Koganei's growers maintain it within the city's heritage vegetable program.

facts.claim_en: Magome three-sun carrot is included in the official list of heritage vegetables cultivated in Koganei.

food_cultures.summary_en: Koganei promotes rhubarb as a newer local specialty. Its tart stalks are turned into jam, compote, confectionery, and educational food projects.

facts.claim_en: Koganei promotes local rhubarb production, and its schools have used rhubarb in jam and madeleines.
JA-affiliated cooking activities in Koganei have introduced rhubarb preparations, and local rhubarb jam is associated with the farmers' market.

food_cultures.season_en: Approximately May–June and October–November in Koganei.
food_cultures.notes_en: Rhubarb's regional importance comes from a newer specialty-crop initiative rather than an Edo-period origin.

food_cultures.summary_en: Urban orchards in Koganei cultivate several kiwifruit varieties, including Hayward, Rainbow Red, and Tokyo Gold. Farm-gate orchards make the city's fruit production tangible to visitors.

facts.claim_en: Hake-no-Michi Orchard grows Hayward and Rainbow Red kiwifruit in Koganei.
Motohashi Orchard grows several kiwifruit varieties and offers kiwi-related processed produce.

food_cultures.summary_en: Sankoin preserves a style of temple vegetarian cuisine influenced by Muromachi-period court food. Its seasonal dishes offer a direct link between Koganei and an older Japanese culinary tradition.

facts.claim_en: Sankoin is a Buddhist nunnery founded in 1934 that preserves Takenogosho-style shojin cuisine derived from courtly food traditions.
facts.source_title: 江戸東京な たてもの探訪

food_cultures.summary_en: Koganei's heritage vegetable movement has also reconstructed historical Tokyo dishes. An Edo-style New Year soup using traditional vegetables was presented as part of a local food-culture event.

facts.claim_en: A Koganei heritage-vegetable event at the Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum presented Edo-style ozoni incorporating traditional greens and Kameido daikon.
facts.source_title: 江戸東京野菜でまちおこし

food_cultures.summary_en: A Koganei wagashi shop maintains a traditional wheat-gluten confection with roots in Kyoto's refined cuisine. It has become a locally cherished sweet.

facts.claim_en: Sanyo preserves a fu-manju technique derived from Kyoto-style formal cooking and presents the confection as a local specialty.

facts.claim_en: A 2013 account documents tomato daifuku and tomato yokan developed using Koganei-grown tomatoes in cooperation with a local confectionery maker.

facts.claim_en: Koganei City identified Chuo Line Beer Works as the city's first craft brewery, established in 2025.

food_cultures.summary_en: Small urban farms sell vegetables and fruit directly to neighbors, preserving a visible relationship between the city and its agricultural land. This is a useful way to encounter seasonal produce beyond conventional restaurants.

facts.claim_en: Koganei City documents produce sold directly from local farms and household-front farm stands.

food_cultures.summary_en: Kodaira identifies itself as the birthplace of commercial blueberry cultivation in Japan. The fruit became a prominent local identity, supported by farms, fruit-picking culture, and processed specialties.

facts.claim_en: Commercial blueberry cultivation began in Kodaira in 1968 through the work of agricultural researcher Iwagaki Hayao.

facts.claim_en: Tokyo's regional-resource program identifies blueberries as a Kodaira specialty connected to local foods and tourism.

facts.claim_en: The city's blueberry wine festival also promotes sweets made with Kodaira-grown blueberries.

food_cultures.summary_en: Blanched udo shoots are a long-established Tokyo vegetable specialty. Kodaira is a notable production area, and the crop represents an older style of metropolitan farming.

facts.claim_en: Kodaira City describes udo as one of its signature agricultural products and a vegetable cultivated in Tokyo since the Edo period.

food_cultures.summary_en: Pear growing became a substantial part of Kodaira's fruit agriculture after the Second World War. Local cultivars create a harvest sequence spanning late summer and autumn.

facts.claim_en: Kodaira City identifies Japanese pears as its leading fruit crop and describes Kosui, Hosui, and Niitaka as important local varieties.

facts.claim_en: Kodaira City explicitly identifies chestnuts among the fruits grown by local farmers.

food_cultures.summary_en: Taro is one of the vegetables specifically highlighted in Kodaira's account of local agriculture. It belongs to the area's everyday farm-produce tradition.

facts.claim_en: Kodaira City names taro as one of the prominent vegetable crops cultivated locally.

food_cultures.notes_en: This is a locally supported crop, not a claim of a Kodaira-exclusive cultivar.

food_cultures.summary_en: Traditional hand-cut wheat noodles are eaten with boiled seasonal vegetables called kate and a concentrated dipping broth. The dish reflects Musashino's dry-field wheat farming and its customs surrounding celebrations and communal meals.

facts.claim_en: Kodaira's kate udon combines handmade wheat noodles, boiled seasonal vegetables, and dipping broth.

food_cultures.summary_en: Tokyo Gosho is a persimmon cultivar developed through Tokyo's agricultural research system. It is among Hino's distinctive autumn fruits.

food_cultures.summary_en: Zenjimaru is a traditional persimmon variety included among the cultivars grown in Hino. It also belongs to Tokyo's broader register of historically significant crops.

facts.claim_en: Hino City lists Zenjimaru among persimmon cultivars grown locally.
Tokyo's Edo-Tokyo crop register includes Zenjimaru persimmon as a reference-listed traditional crop.

food_cultures.notes_en: The traditional cultivar is not exclusive to Hino.

food_cultures.summary_en: Hino has revived a beer with roots in an unusually early local brewing enterprise. The modern project connects archaeological and industrial history with a contemporary regional beverage.

facts.claim_en: Toyoda Beer was historically brewed in Hino between 1886 and 1894 and was revived through a local heritage project in 2015.
facts.source_title: TOYODA BEER プロジェクト

facts.claim_en: The revival project worked with Ishikawa Shuzo in neighboring Fussa, drawing on historical ties between brewing families.

food_cultures.notes_en: Historical brewing in Hino and present-day production arrangements should not be conflated.

food_cultures.name_en: Beer made entirely with Hino-grown barley
food_cultures.summary_en: A related local agriculture-and-brewing initiative uses barley grown in Hino. It is distinct from the general Toyoda Beer historical revival because the crop itself becomes a central part of the product story.

facts.claim_en: Local farmers began growing barley for beer in 2014, and Premium Toyoda Beer made entirely with Hino barley was produced from 2018 through 2022.
facts.publisher: TOYODA BEER プロジェクト

facts.claim_en: Although Premium Toyoda Beer ended, the project reports continuing beer production using entirely Hino-grown barley through local growers and community groups.
